title: Theory
text:
For penalized coefficients \(\beta\) and optional unpenalized coefficients \(\theta\), SPARES uses
\[
\frac{1}{2n}\|y-X\beta-Z\theta\|_2^2+\lambda P(\beta;y).
\]
Weights are held fixed while optimizing over coefficients. For adaptive penalties they depend on the response and must be differentiated when studying the fitted-value map. A formulation with loss \(\|y-X\beta-Z\theta\|^2/2\) uses \(\gamma=n\lambda\).

title: Theory
text:
For penalized coefficients \(\beta\) and optional unpenalized coefficients \(\theta\), SPARES uses
\[
\frac{1}{2n}\|y-X\beta-Z\theta\|_2^2+\lambda P(\beta;y).
\]
Weights are held fixed while optimizing over coefficients. For adaptive penalties they depend on the response and must be differentiated when studying the fitted-value map. A formulation with loss \(\|y-X\beta-Z\theta\|^2/2\) uses \(\gamma=n\lambda\).

title: Theory
text:
2 Adaptive weights
The inverse-weight adaptive approach is developed by Zou (2006) for scalar coefficients and by Wang and Leng (2008) for groups.
Write \(r_g(y)=\|\widehat\beta_g^{\mathrm{LS}}(y)\|_2\) and \(w_g(y)=\omega_g(r_g(y))\). For scalar groups the radius is the absolute value of the pilot coefficient. Typical profiles are
\[
\omega_g(r)=r^{-a},\qquad \omega_g(r)=e^{-ar},\qquad a>0.
\]
The profile derivative is taken with respect to \(r\); differentiation with respect to \(y\) additionally uses the chain rule through the pilot. Singular profiles require an extended-value penalty convention at zero, as explained under Degrees of freedom.

title: Theory
section: 3 Degrees of freedom and Stein’s identity
text:
3 Degrees of freedom and Stein’s identity
The following definitions connect Stein’s identity (Stein 1981) to covariance-based prediction-error corrections (Efron 2004).
Under \(Y\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2I_n)\) with \(\sigma^2>0\), define
\[
\mathrm{df}(\widehat\mu_\lambda)=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}
\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Cov}(Y_i,\widehat\mu_{\lambda,i}(Y)).
\]
At a fixed deterministic \(\lambda\), suitable weak differentiability and Gaussian integrability conditions allow Stein’s identity:
\[
\mathrm{df}(\widehat\mu_\lambda)
=\mathbb E\!\left[\operatorname{tr}\{D_y\widehat\mu_\lambda(Y)\}\right].
\]
The divergence is a function of the observed response. Its computation is local; the expectation identity also requires global regularity and integrability. Differentiability almost everywhere alone does not establish the identity.

title: Theory
text:
4 Active penalty curvature
Group-penalty geometry is central to the Group Lasso (Yuan and Lin 2006); a general sensitivity and degrees-of-freedom framework for partly smooth regularizers is given by Vaiter et al. (2017).
For a fixed positive group weight and a nonzero active group coefficient, the Hessian block of the group penalty is
\[
\Pi_g=\frac{w_g}{\|\widehat\beta_g\|_2}
\left(I_{n_g}-\frac{\widehat\beta_g\widehat\beta_g^\top}{\|\widehat\beta_g\|_2^2}\right).
\]
It vanishes in the coefficient direction and contracts orthogonal directions. Adaptive weights add a response-derivative term to the differentiated optimality equations. Consequently, simply counting selected coefficients generally misses both group shrinkage and the contribution of adaptation.

title: Theory
text:
5 Scope of interpretation
The distinction between fitting and model search is discussed by Tibshirani (2015); for the Lasso degrees-of-freedom identity, see Zou, Hastie, and Tibshirani (2007).
The package evaluates local divergence and checks numerical conditions needed for that calculation. The Gaussian unbiasedness interpretation requires the corresponding regularity assumptions; it is not asserted automatically for every adaptive overlap or sparse variant. Selecting \(\lambda\) using the same response defines another fitting rule, whose complexity is not automatically estimated by the fixed-\(\lambda\) divergence.
The model-selection guide describes the implemented criteria, including the role of known versus estimated noise variance. This page is an overview of the implementation’s mathematical conventions, not a replacement for a complete proof of its regularity hypotheses.

section: 2 Generate data with a known structure
text:
2 Generate data with a known structure
There are twelve correlated predictors in four disjoint groups of size three. Only the first two groups contain signal; the second contains both nonzero and zero coefficients. This illustrates the distinction between selecting a group and selecting every coordinate individually.

set.seed(2026)
n <- 100
p <- 12
groups <- rep(1:4, each = 3)
Sigma <- outer(seq_len(p), seq_len(p), function(i, j) 0.35^abs(i-j))
X <- matrix(rnorm(n*p), n, p) %*% chol(Sigma)
colnames(X) <- paste0('x', seq_len(p))
beta_true <- c(1.5, -1, 0.8, 1, -0.7, 0, rep(0, 6))
intercept_true <- 1
sigma <- 0.8
mu <- as.numeric(intercept_true + X %*% beta_true)
y <- mu + rnorm(n, sd = sigma)

                       coefficient=beta_true), digits=2)

Predictors have the same population variance. We do not standardize them in this example: the design matrix is held fixed throughout fitting and the numerical derivative check. An unpenalized intercept is included in every fit. The OLS pilot is identifiable because the full design has full column rank and \(n>p+1\).

2.1 A common positive grid

lambda <- 10^seq(1, -2.5, length.out = 60)
control <- list(maxit=20000, abstol=1e-10, reltol=1e-10, print.out=FALSE)

This geometric grid spans strong to weak regularization. It is specified before looking at the response and reused for all methods. The upper end should produce an intercept-only fit; we check this rather than assuming it. For routine analyses, automatic grids and lambdamax() are also available.

title: Estimates and degrees of freedom along the path
text:
3 Lasso and Adaptive Lasso
The Lasso uses fixed coordinate weights. Adaptive Lasso uses the full-design OLS pilot with exponential weights \(\omega_j(r)=e^{-r}\). Large pilot magnitudes receive smaller penalties. This finite profile also avoids a singular weight at a zero pilot; inverse-power weights are covered in the workflow vignette.

fit_lasso <- lmreg(X, y, penalty='lasso', intercept=TRUE,
                   standardize=FALSE, lambda=lambda, control=control)
fit_adalasso <- lmreg(X, y, penalty='adalasso', profile='exponential',
                      exponent=1, intercept=TRUE, standardize=FALSE,
                      lambda=lambda, control=control)
fits <- list('Lasso'=fit_lasso, 'Adaptive Lasso'=fit_adalasso)


3.1 Extract estimates and check diagnostics
beta has one row per penalized variable and one column per regularization value. a0 stores the intercept path; coef() includes it in coefficient extraction. dof() returns one row per regularization value, including the status of the derivative calculation.

path_data <- function(fit, method) {
  data.frame(method=method, lambda=rep(fit$lambda, each=nrow(fit$beta)),
             variable=factor(rep(colnames(X), times=length(fit$lambda)), levels=colnames(X)),
             estimate=as.vector(fit$beta),
             group=factor(rep(groups, times=length(fit$lambda))))
}
coefficient_plot <- function(fits) {
  dat <- do.call(rbind, Map(path_data, fits, names(fits)))
  ggplot(dat, aes(lambda, estimate, colour=variable, group=variable)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept=0, colour='grey80') + geom_line(linewidth=0.6) +
    scale_x_log10() + facet_wrap(~method, ncol=2) +
    labs(x=expression(lambda), y=expression(hat(beta)[j]), colour='Variable') +
    theme(legend.position='bottom', legend.box='vertical') +
    guides(colour=guide_legend(nrow=2, byrow=TRUE, order=1))
}
get_diagnostics <- function(fits) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(m) {
    d <- dof(fits[[m]])
    data.frame(method=m, lambda=d$lambda, df=d$df,
               status=d$status, nzero=fits[[m]]$nzero)
  }))
}
diagnostics <- get_diagnostics(fits)
knitr::kable(as.data.frame(table(diagnostics$method, diagnostics$status)),

3.2 Coefficient paths

coefficient_plot(fits)




Coefficient paths for Lasso and Adaptive Lasso. Colours identify the same variables in both panels; the intercept is omitted.




At the right-hand end, the penalized coefficients are zero. Moving left relaxes the penalty and allows signal variables, and eventually noise variables, into the model. Compare how quickly the large signal coefficients approach their true values under adaptive weighting. Their values at specific knots are shown next, so that the comparison is not based on visual impressions alone.

coefficient_slices <- function(fits, indices=c(1, 25, 45, 60)) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(m) {
    f <- fits[[m]]
    b <- coef(f, s=f$lambda[indices])
    z <- data.frame(variable=rownames(b), truth=c(intercept_true, beta_true), b,
                    check.names=FALSE)
    names(z)[-(1:2)] <- paste0('lambda=', format(signif(f$lambda[indices],3), trim=TRUE))
    cbind(method=m, z)
  }))
}

3.3 Degrees of freedom along the same paths
With an intercept and a full-column-rank design, the fixed-weight Lasso reference is \(1+|A|\): the intercept contributes one degree of freedom. For Adaptive Lasso the total also includes derivatives of the pilot-based weights. We compare each method with its own active set.

plot_dof <- function(d) {
  z <- rbind(data.frame(d, quantity='Divergence', value=d$df),
             data.frame(d, quantity='1 + nonzero coefficients', value=1+d$nzero))
  ggplot(z, aes(lambda, value, colour=quantity, linetype=quantity)) +
    geom_line(linewidth=0.7) + geom_point(size=0.7) + scale_x_log10() +
    facet_wrap(~method, ncol=2) +
    labs(x=expression(lambda), y='Complexity', colour=NULL, linetype=NULL) +
    theme(legend.position='bottom')
}

title: Estimates and degrees of freedom along the path
section: 4 Group Lasso and Adaptive Group Lasso
text:
4 Group Lasso and Adaptive Group Lasso
We now use the known disjoint groups. The data, intercept and regularization grid stay the same. Group Lasso promotes entire groups entering or leaving the model; it does not generally create sparsity within an active group.

fit_glasso <- lmreg(X, y, penalty='glasso', groups=groups,
                    intercept=TRUE, standardize=FALSE,
                    lambda=lambda, control=control)
fit_adaglasso <- lmreg(X, y, penalty='adaglasso', groups=groups,
                       profile='exponential', exponent=1,
                       intercept=TRUE, standardize=FALSE,
                       lambda=lambda, control=control)
group_fits <- list('Group Lasso'=fit_glasso, 'Adaptive Group Lasso'=fit_adaglasso)
group_diagnostics <- get_diagnostics(group_fits)
stopifnot(all(group_diagnostics$status == 'ok'))
knitr::kable(as.data.frame(table(group_diagnostics$method, group_diagnostics$status)),
             col.names=c('Method','Derivative status','Grid points'))

4.1 Coordinate estimates and group norms

coefficient_plot(group_fits)




Individual coefficient estimates along the group-penalized paths. These are coefficients, not group norms.





group_path <- function(fit, method) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(unique(groups), function(g) {
    data.frame(method=method, lambda=fit$lambda, group=factor(g),
               norm=sqrt(colSums(fit$beta[groups==g,,drop=FALSE]^2)),
               truth=sqrt(sum(beta_true[groups==g]^2)))
  }))
}
gp <- do.call(rbind, Map(group_path, group_fits, names(group_fits)))
truths <- unique(gp[c('method','group','truth')])
ggplot(gp, aes(lambda, norm, colour=group)) + geom_line(linewidth=0.7) +
  geom_hline(data=truths, aes(yintercept=truth, colour=group), linetype=3) +
  scale_x_log10() + facet_wrap(~method, ncol=2) +
  labs(x=expression(lambda), y=expression(group~norm~~rho[g]), colour='Group') +
  theme(legend.position='bottom')




Estimated group norms along the path. The dashed horizontal levels are the true group norms; colours identify groups consistently.




The true norm is zero for groups 3 and 4. Their fitted norms show when weak regularization admits groups containing only noise. Group 2 contains a truly zero coordinate, but its group is informative: selecting this group does not imply that all three of its coefficients are truly nonzero.

4.2 Group counts, dimensions and divergence

group_counts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(group_fits), function(m) {
  f <- group_fits[[m]]; d <- dof(f)
  active <- attr(d, 'active_groups')
  ng <- d$active_groups
  dimension <- vapply(active, function(a) sum(table(groups)[a]), numeric(1))
  rbind(data.frame(method=m,lambda=f$lambda,quantity='Divergence',value=d$df),
        data.frame(method=m,lambda=f$lambda,quantity='1 + nonzero coefficients',value=1+f$nzero),
        data.frame(method=m,lambda=f$lambda,quantity='1 + active groups',value=1+ng),
        data.frame(method=m,lambda=f$lambda,quantity='1 + active-group dimension',value=1+dimension))
}))
ggplot(group_counts, aes(lambda,value,colour=quantity,linetype=quantity)) +
  geom_line(linewidth=0.7) + scale_x_log10() + facet_wrap(~method,ncol=2) +
  labs(x=expression(lambda), y='Complexity', colour=NULL,linetype=NULL) +
  theme(legend.position='bottom') +
  guides(colour=guide_legend(nrow=2,byrow=TRUE),
         linetype=guide_legend(nrow=2,byrow=TRUE))




Total divergence, number of nonzero coordinates, active-group count and active-group dimension. Each count includes the intercept contribution.




Counts use the active groups returned by dof(), whose diagnostics distinguish constrained-zero groups from small numerical residuals. Testing raw fitted coefficients for exact equality to zero can give misleading counts.
For fixed positive group weights, the penalized divergence lies between the number of active groups and their total dimension; the plotted totals add the intercept. The active-group dimension counts all coordinates in active groups, including any individually zero coefficients. The two coordinate-count curves may overlap in this example. Adaptive weight derivatives introduce another term, so the fixed-weight bounds should not be transferred unchanged to the adaptive total.


4.3 Decompose the adaptive divergence

all_fits <- c(fits, group_fits)
adaptive_fits <- all_fits[c('Adaptive Lasso','Adaptive Group Lasso')]
components <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(adaptive_fits), function(m) {
 d <- dof(adaptive_fits[[m]])
 rbind(data.frame(method=m,lambda=d$lambda,component='Total',value=d$df),
       data.frame(method=m,lambda=d$lambda,component='Fixed-weight contribution',value=d$df_fixed),
       data.frame(method=m,lambda=d$lambda,component='Adaptive correction',value=d$adaptive_correction))
}))
ggplot(components,aes(lambda,value,colour=component,linetype=component)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept=0,colour='grey80') + geom_line(linewidth=0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() + facet_wrap(~method,ncol=2) +
  labs(x=expression(lambda),y='Divergence contribution',colour=NULL,linetype=NULL) +
  theme(legend.position='bottom')




Decomposition at the adaptive solutions: total divergence equals the fixed-weight contribution plus the adaptive correction.




The fixed-weight contribution is computed at the same adaptive solution, with the observed weights held constant only during differentiation. It is not the DoF of the separately fitted ordinary Lasso or Group Lasso. The correction excludes the intercept contribution, which is already included in the fixed-weight term.

title: Estimates and degrees of freedom along the path
section: 5 Select a location on each path
text:
5 Select a location on each path
For each method, we compute effective-DoF BIC, known-variance SURE, and five-fold CV with a common fold assignment and an explicit common grid. The adaptive pilot is recomputed in every training fold. Using the true variance in SURE is possible here because this is a simulation.

set.seed(2027)
foldid <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out=n))
penalties <- c('lasso','adalasso','glasso','adaglasso')
selected <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(all_fits), function(i) {
 m <- names(all_fits)[i]; f <- all_fits[[i]]
 bic <- select(f, criterion='BIC')
 sure <- select(f, criterion='SURE', sigma2=sigma^2)
 args <- list(X=X,y=y,penalty=penalties[i],intercept=TRUE,
              standardize=FALSE,lambda=lambda,foldid=foldid,control=control)
 if(i>=3) args$groups <- groups
 if(i %in% c(2,4)) {args$profile <- 'exponential'; args$exponent <- 1}
 cv <- do.call(cv.lmreg,args)
 data.frame(method=m,rule=c('BIC','SURE','CV minimum','CV one SE'),
            lambda=c(bic$lambda,sure$lambda,cv$lambda.min,cv$lambda.1se))
}))

  labs(x=expression(lambda),y='Divergence',linetype='Selection rule') +
  theme(legend.position='bottom')




The same tuning choices located on the divergence paths. These are fixed-lambda divergences evaluated at selected knots, not DoF estimates for the entire selection procedure.




BIC, SURE and CV target different criteria and need not select the same knot. The one-SE choice favours a larger penalty than the CV minimum according to the reported fold-dispersion rule. It is not an exact uncertainty statement accounting for overlapping training sets. The fixed-\(\lambda\) unbiasedness result does not automatically apply to the full data-dependent selection rule.


5.2 Evaluate on independent test observations

performance <- do.call(rbind,lapply(seq_len(nrow(selected)),function(i) {
 s <- selected[i,]; f <- all_fits[[s$method]]
 pred <- as.numeric(predict(f,newx=Xtest,s=s$lambda))
 k <- which.min(abs(f$lambda-s$lambda))
 data.frame(s,nonzero=f$nzero[k],df=dof(f)$df[k],
            mean_MSE=mean((pred-mutest)^2),prediction_MSE=mean((pred-ytest)^2))
}))

title: Estimates and degrees of freedom along the path
text:
6 Check the analytic divergence numerically
Stein’s expectation identity requires regularity and integrability (Stein 1981). Relevant degrees-of-freedom results include those for the Lasso (Zou, Hastie, and Tibshirani 2007) and partly smooth regularizers (Vaiter et al. 2017). The finite-difference calculation below checks a local Jacobian formula; it does not prove those global hypotheses.
For one fixed Adaptive Group Lasso knot, approximate \(\sum_i\partial\widehat\mu_i/\partial y_i\) by centered response perturbations. We refit the adaptive model for every perturbation, including recomputation of its pilot and weights. Holding the weights fixed would check a different Jacobian. The design, regularization value and preprocessing are held fixed.

f <- fit_adaglasso
k <- which.min(abs(f$lambda-0.1))
lambda_check <- f$lambda[k]
refit_mean <- function(response) {
 fit <- lmreg(X,response,penalty='adaglasso',groups=groups,
              profile='exponential',exponent=1,intercept=TRUE,
              standardize=FALSE,lambda=lambda_check,control=control)
 stopifnot(all(as.numeric(fit$convergence)==1))
 as.numeric(predict(fit,newx=X))
}
finite_difference <- function(h) {
 sum(vapply(seq_len(n),function(i) {
   yp <- ym <- y; yp[i] <- yp[i]+h; ym[i] <- ym[i]-h
   (refit_mean(yp)[i]-refit_mean(ym)[i])/(2*h)
 },numeric(1)))
}
h <- c(1e-3,3e-4)
analytic <- dof(f)$df[k]
fd <- vapply(h,finite_difference,numeric(1))
validation <- data.frame(lambda=lambda_check,step=h,analytic=analytic,
                         numerical=fd,absolute_error=abs(fd-analytic))
validation_display <- validation
validation_display$absolute_error <- formatC(validation$absolute_error, format='e', digits=2)
knitr::kable(validation_display,digits=7,row.names=FALSE)

A connected workflow
fit <- lmreg(X, y, penalty = "adaglasso", groups = groups,
             profile = "exponential", intercept = TRUE)

title: SPARES
text:
Reading this documentation
Start with Getting started, then use Methods to choose a penalty. Degrees of freedom explains diagnostics and adaptive weights; Model selection covers AIC, BIC, SURE and cross-validation. Benchmarks reports reproducible numerical comparisons and their scope.
The worked examples are generated from the package vignette, keeping the installed tutorial and the website aligned. This site documents the current linear-regression implementation.

title: Degrees of freedom
text:
The following example uses the adaptive Group Lasso fit from Getting started. Degrees of freedom include the response dependence of the adaptive weights.

fit$dof <- dof(fit)
fit$dof
#>   lambda       df df_fixed adaptive_correction active_size active_groups
#> 1   0.30 4.979842 4.770734          0.20910803           4             2
#> 2   0.15 4.989652 4.885030          0.10462206           4             2
#> 3   0.07 6.414050 6.296359          0.11769075           6             3
#> 4   0.03 6.767343 6.715623          0.05171951           6             3
#>   rank_unpenalized df_penalized converged    kkt_error status
#> 1                1     3.979842      TRUE 8.729311e-09     ok
#> 2                1     3.989652      TRUE 4.315088e-09     ok
#> 3                1     5.414050      TRUE 3.997284e-09     ok
#> 4                1     5.767343      TRUE 2.230734e-09     ok

nzero counts coefficients; dof() computes divergence. The fixed-weight contribution is evaluated at the same adaptive solution, rather than at another fit with independently chosen weights. Numerical failures or unresolved boundary diagnostics are reported rather than silently treated as reliable derivatives.
See Theory for the distinction between divergence and Gaussian unbiasedness, and Model selection for the use of these values in criteria.
For the Lasso identity, see Zou, Hastie, and Tibshirani (2007); for partly smooth regularizers, see Vaiter et al. (2017). The Gaussian expectation identity requires Stein’s regularity and integrability hypotheses (Stein 1981). ## Zero pilots and singular weights
For inverse powers, a zero pilot radius produces an infinite weight. SPARES then imposes exact zero coefficients for that coordinate or every coordinate of that group. Shared coordinates in overlapping groups are constrained too. The remaining problem is solved on the free coordinates, retaining the original full-pilot derivatives. No large finite replacement or epsilon perturbation is used. An explicit positive lambda grid is currently required at singular zero pilots. Exactly zero is distinguished from very small.

zfit <- adalasso(diag(4),c(0,2,3,0),lambda=c(.1,.2),control=control)
zfit$beta
#>          s0       s1
#> X1 0.000000 0.000000
#> X2 1.800000 1.600000
#> X3 2.866667 2.733333
#> X4 0.000000 0.000000
dof(zfit)
#>   lambda df converged                     status
#> 1    0.1  0      TRUE exceptional_set_convention
#> 2    0.2  0      TRUE exceptional_set_convention

Finite profiles are evaluated at zero through their supplied extension (e.g. exponential weights equal one there). At any exactly zero pilot radius, dof() returns the declared exceptional-set value zero, labelled exceptional_set_convention; this is not a claim of a classical derivative at that response. Nonconverged fits still receive NA. Selection excludes such convention-only values rather than using them as complexity estimates. Custom profiles must define their values at zero, allowing positive infinity for a singular profile.

title: Numerical checks and benchmarks
text:
Package tests compare local divergence with centered response perturbations, recomputing adaptive weights on each refit. They cover inactive overlaps, unpenalized covariates, sparse endpoints, scaling, zero-pilot conventions, CV fold isolation and criteria formulas.
The installed benchmark script compares Lasso and adaptive Lasso with glmnet, and Group Lasso and adaptive Group Lasso with gglasso:

system.file('benchmarks','compare_reference.R',package='spares')

Run that script separately to obtain coefficient/prediction discrepancies, median elapsed times and session information. Designs, penalties, scales, intercepts and lambda values are matched; the adaptive Lasso comparison compensates for glmnet’s normalization of penalty factors. Times include wrapper overhead and exclude DoF calculation. These small warm-run examples are numerical checks, not evidence of universal speed superiority. Overlap and sparse adaptive methods are validated by KKT and derivative tests rather than claimed to match a different latent-overlap objective.
A recorded run bundled with this release gives the following results; re-run the script for timings on your machine.

title: Getting started
text:
2 One interface, different penalties
The Lasso (Tibshirani 1996), Group Lasso (Yuan and Lin 2006) and sparse-group Lasso (Simon et al. 2013) motivate the main penalty families. Structured sparsity with overlapping groups is discussed by Jenatton, Audibert, and Bach (2011); adaptive weighting originates in the Adaptive Lasso (Zou 2006) and its group extension (Wang and Leng 2008). For a broader treatment, see Hastie, Tibshirani, and Wainwright (2015). These references describe the underlying methods; they do not establish every extension implemented in SPARES.
Estimation uses ADMM; its general framework and convergence conditions are reviewed by Boyd et al. (2011).
SPARES fits Lasso, Group Lasso, overlapping-group and sparse-group paths, with fixed or least-squares-pilot-based adaptive weights. The loss is \(\|y-X\beta-Z\theta\|^2/(2n)\), so the parameter called \(\gamma\) in an unnormalized RSS/2 objective is \(n\lambda\).

set.seed(21)
n <- 60
X <- matrix(rnorm(n*6),n,6)
colnames(X) <- paste0('x',1:6)
y <- as.numeric(1+X%*%c(1.5,-1,.7,0,0,0)+rnorm(n,sd=.5))
groups <- rep(1:3,each=2)
control <- list(maxit=10000,abstol=1e-9,reltol=1e-9,print.out=FALSE)
fit <- lmreg(X,y,penalty='adaglasso',groups=groups,profile='exponential',
             intercept=TRUE,standardize=TRUE,
             lambda=c(.3,.15,.07,.03),control=control)
print(fit)
#> SPARES: adaptive glasso
#> 60 observations; 6 penalized predictors; 0 additional unpenalized predictors
#>  lambda nzero converged
#>    0.30     4      TRUE
#>    0.15     4      TRUE
#>    0.07     6      TRUE
#>    0.03     6      TRUE

standardize=TRUE scales predictors by sample standard deviations and centers them only when an intercept is requested. It does not standardize the response or the supplied unpenalized covariates Z. Adaptive pilots, weights and penalties refer to these working coefficient coordinates; changing scales generally changes the penalty. Coefficients and predictions are transformed back to original units. All preprocessing is retained. The legacy standardize.data=TRUE scales the response as well and cannot be combined with standardize=TRUE; it is still excluded from DoF calculations.

coef(fit,s=.07)
#>                    s=0.07
#> (Intercept)  1.0707681857
#> x1           1.5499944953
#> x2          -1.0303063568
#> x3           0.7087414216
#> x4          -0.0005907048
#> x5           0.0331123454
#> x6          -0.0057908462
predict(fit,newx=X[1:3,,drop=FALSE],s=.07)
#>         s=0.07
#> [1,] 2.4933851
#> [2,] 0.4859352
#> [3,] 6.0129774
plot(fit,xvar='loglambda',label=TRUE)








A lambda between fitted knots uses linear interpolation, not an exact refit. Without s, extraction and prediction return the whole fitted path. With unpenalized covariates, pass the matching newz at prediction time; an intercept requested by intercept=TRUE is added automatically.

title: Methods
text:
2 Weights and regularization grids
Adaptive methods use a full-design least-squares pilot and support inverse-power, exponential and user-defined profiles with their derivatives. An identifiable pilot is required, including within each cross-validation training fold.
lambdamax() provides method-specific thresholds or certified upper bounds for constructing grids. Supply lambda to use your own grid; exactly zero pilot radii with singular weights currently require an explicit positive grid.

title: Methods
text:
3 Fitted objects and predictions

coef(fit) extracts the coefficient path; coef(fit, s = ...) selects a regularization value.
predict(fit, newx = ..., s = ...) predicts on new observations; supply newz when the model includes unpenalized covariates.
plot(fit, xvar = "loglambda") displays the path.
dof(fit) evaluates local divergence, with convergence and KKT diagnostics.

Between fitted knots, extraction uses linear interpolation rather than an exact optimization refit. Without s, extraction returns the whole path. The number of nonzero coefficients, nzero, is distinct from effective degrees of freedom.

title: Methods
text:
4 Scaling
standardize = TRUE scales predictors by sample standard deviations and centers them when an intercept is fitted. Coefficients and predictions are returned on the original scale, but penalties and adaptive pilots are defined in the working coordinates. The response and supplied unpenalized covariates are not scaled.
The legacy standardize.data option also rescales the response and is not supported by the DoF calculations. See the worked example for the supported workflow.

title: Methods
text:
5 Function documentation in R
Use ?lmreg, ?lambdamax, ?dof, ?select, ?cv.lmreg and ?spares for argument definitions, return values and method-specific details.

title: Model selection
text:
The covariance definition of degrees of freedom and prediction-error corrections provide the statistical background (Efron 2004). Stein’s identity (Stein 1981) relates divergence to Gaussian degrees of freedom under suitable regularity and integrability conditions. For the Lasso, see Zou, Hastie, and Tibshirani (2007); for partly smooth regularizers, including the fixed-weight Group Lasso, see Vaiter et al. (2017).
AIC (Akaike 1974) and BIC (Schwarz 1978) motivate the information criteria below. Substituting an effective divergence into these criteria does not transfer all their classical guarantees to an arbitrary adaptive penalized fit.

fit$dof <- dof(fit)
fit$dof
#>   lambda       df df_fixed adaptive_correction active_size active_groups
#> 1   0.30 4.979842 4.770734          0.20910803           4             2
#> 2   0.15 4.989652 4.885030          0.10462206           4             2
#> 3   0.07 6.414050 6.296359          0.11769075           6             3
#> 4   0.03 6.767343 6.715623          0.05171951           6             3
#>   rank_unpenalized df_penalized converged    kkt_error status
#> 1                1     3.979842      TRUE 8.729311e-09     ok
#> 2                1     3.989652      TRUE 4.315088e-09     ok
#> 3                1     5.414050      TRUE 3.997284e-09     ok
#> 4                1     5.767343      TRUE 2.230734e-09     ok
chosen <- select(fit,criterion='BIC')
print(chosen)
#> SPARES selection by BIC 
#> Selected lambda: 0.15 
#> Variance: profiled per candidate 
#>  lambda      rss       df     score eligible status
#>    0.30 14.90010 4.979842 -59.09505     TRUE     ok
#>    0.15 13.86996 4.989652 -63.35345     TRUE     ok
#>    0.07 13.26736 6.414050 -60.18659     TRUE     ok
#>    0.03 12.97666 6.767343 -60.06937     TRUE     ok
predict(chosen,newx=X[1:3,,drop=FALSE])
#>        s=0.15
#> [1,] 2.545932
#> [2,] 0.534954
#> [3,] 5.955573
plot(chosen)








The coefficient count nzero is distinct from divergence. The latter includes penalty curvature and derivatives of adaptive weights. In grouped and adaptive output, df_fixed is evaluated at the same adaptive solution; it is not the complexity of another separately fitted model.
For \(d_\lambda=\widehat{\mathrm{df}}_\lambda\) and residual sum of squares \(R_\lambda\), the profiled criteria implemented when sigma2=NULL are
[ =n(R/n)+2(d_+1), =n(R/n)+(n)(d_+1). ]
The extra parameter is the estimated variance; common likelihood constants are omitted. These substitute effective complexity for parameter count: they do not assert ordinary maximum-likelihood AIC or BIC theory for every penalized candidate. See the R documentation for AIC for the underlying likelihood convention.
With a supplied variance \(v\), the likelihood term becomes \(R_\lambda/v\) and the variance parameter is not counted. SURE for mean estimation is
[ R_/n+2v d_/n-v. ]

sure <- select(fit,criterion='SURE',sigma2=.5^2)
sure$lambda
#> [1] 0.03
plugin <- select(fit,criterion='SURE',sigma2='ols')
plugin$variance_source
#> [1] "full-design OLS plug-in"

"ols" uses the full design and requires positive residual degrees of freedom. It is a plug-in criterion, not an exact known-variance SURE identity. Known-variance unbiasedness requires Gaussian errors and the relevant global regularity/integrability hypotheses; a numerical local divergence does not establish those hypotheses for adaptive overlap and sparse variants. Nor does unbiasedness at fixed lambda extend automatically to a selected fit. Failed diagnostics and exceptional-set conventions are excluded from selection.

title: Model selection
text:
2 Cross-validation without pilot leakage
Cross-validation and prediction-error estimation are discussed by Hastie, Tibshirani, and Wainwright (2015) and Efron (2004). Model search can contribute additional degrees of freedom (Tibshirani 2015), so a divergence computed at a fixed tuning value is not automatically the degrees of freedom of the data-selected procedure.

foldid <- rep(1:3,length.out=n)
cv <- cv.lmreg(X,y,foldid=foldid,penalty='adaglasso',groups=groups,
              profile='exponential',intercept=TRUE,standardize=TRUE,
              lambda=c(.3,.15,.07,.03),control=control)
print(cv)
#> SPARES cross-validation; alignment: lambda 
#>     rule lambda       mse
#>  minimum   0.07 0.2818870
#>   one-SE   0.30 0.3110961
plot(cv)







coef(cv,s='lambda.1se')
#>                     s=0.3
#> (Intercept)  1.062105e+00
#> x1           1.526346e+00
#> x2          -1.012827e+00
#> x3           5.910858e-01
#> x4          -5.559435e-03
#> x5          -4.291376e-10
#> x6          -5.713648e-10

Each training fold computes its own scales, OLS pilot and adaptive weights. Reuse foldid to compare methods. Supplied weight vectors must be fixed; passing weights calculated from the full response would introduce leakage. CV assesses prediction error and does not use DoF. Rank requirements for adaptive pilots must hold in each training fold, not just in the full data.
lambda.min minimizes pooled out-of-fold squared error. lambda.1se is the largest candidate within one displayed standard error of that minimum. The standard error is a between-fold dispersion summary, not an exact sampling uncertainty accounting for overlapping training sets.
If no absolute grid is supplied, each fold constructs its own automatic geometric grid; candidates are aligned by the same fraction of each fold’s maximum lambda. No full-data response is used to set training-fold grids. The reported lambdas then refer to the full-data refit. This distinction between absolute lambda and path-relative alignment is also discussed in glmnet’s cross-validation documentation.
